Boiss.|author=|date=n.d.|website=Plants of the World Online|publisher=The Trustees of the Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|access-date= 18 September 2020}} }} '''''Picea smithiana''''' is a species of [[evergreen]] tree in the family [[Pinaceae]] family. It is referred to by the common names '''morinda spruce'''{{BSBI 2007 |access-date=2014-10-17 }}{{GRIN |access-date=2018-08-09}}{{cite encyclopedia |editor-last=Huxley |editor-first=A. |title=The new Royal Horticultural Society dictionary of gardening |date=1992}} and '''West Himalayan spruce''', and is a [[spruce]] native to the western [[Himalaya]] and adjacent mountains, from northeast [[Afghanistan|Afghanistan, northern Pakistan]], [[India]] to central [[Nepal]]. It grows at altitudes of {{Convert|2,400-3,600|m|abbr=on}} in forests together with [[deodar cedar]], [[blue pine]] and [[pindrow fir]]. ==Description== [[File:New growth of Himalayan or Morinda Spruce Picea smithiana.JPG|thumb|left|New growth, showing the long needles]] ''Picea smithiana'' is a large [[tree]], an [[evergreen]] growing to {{Convert|40-55|m|abbr=|sp=us}} tall, exceptionally to {{Convert|60|m|abbr=on}}, and with a trunk diameter of up to {{Convert|1-2|m|abbr=on}}. It has a [[cone (geometry)|conical]] crown with level branches and usually pendulous branchlets. The shoots are pale buff-brown, and glabrous (hairless). The [[leaf|leaves]] are needle-like, the longest of any spruce, {{Convert|3-5|cm|abbr=on}} long, rhombic in cross-section, mid-green with inconspicuous [[stomata]]l lines. The [[conifer cone|cones]] are broad cylindric-conic, {{Convert|9-16|cm|abbr=on}} long and 3 cm broad, green when young, maturing buff-brown and opening to 5–6 cm broad 5–7 months after pollination; the scales are stiff and smoothly rounded. Morinda spruce is a popular ornamental tree in large gardens in western Europe for its attractive pendulous branchlets. It is also grown to a small extent in [[forestry]] for [[timber]] and paper production, though its slower growth compared to [[Norway spruce]] reduces its importance outside of its native range. The name ''morinda'' derives from the tree's name in [[Nepali language|Nepali]].{{Cite web |title=Picea smithiana - Plant Finder |url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=285035&isprofile=0&cv |access-date=2024-03-10 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}} ==Etymology== ''Picea'' means 'pitch', and is derived from the ancient [[Latin]] word of the same meaning, {{Lang|la|pix}}. The name is in reference to the sticky sap produced by members of this genus.Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback). pp. 302, ''Smithiana'' is named for [[James Edward Smith (botanist)|James Edward Smith]], an English botanist and the founder of the [[Linnaean Society]]. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== *[https://www.conifers.org/pi/Picea_smithiana.php Gymnosperm Database] {{Taxonbar|from=Q1548216}} [[Category:Picea|smithiana]] [[Category:Trees of Afghanistan]] [[Category:Flora of West Himalaya]] [[Category:Trees of Nepal]] [[Category:Trees of Pakistan]] [[Category:Least concern plants]] [[Category:Taxa named by Pierre Edmond Boissier]] [[Category:Taxa named by Nathaniel Wallich]]
